hints: Recall what the volt measures: potential difference as energy transferred per unit charge passing a point.
Write the defining equation $V = W/Q$ and identify the unit of energy $W$ and the unit of charge $Q$.
Check which pair gives $\text{joule per coulomb}$ and matches the unit $\text{V} = \text{J C}^{-1}$.
walkthrough: Identify the quantity: the volt $\text{V}$ is the unit of potential difference $V$.
State the defining rule: potential difference is work done per unit charge, $V = W/Q$.
Identify the component units: work $W$ is measured in joule $\text{J}$ and charge $Q$ is measured in coulomb $\text{C}$.
Combine them: $1 \text{ V} = 1 \text{ J}$ per $1 \text{ C}$, so $\text{V} = \text{J C}^{-1}$.
Compare with the options: only the coulomb and joule pair matches this definition. This is option B

options.A: Ampere and ohm can be combined as $V = IR$, but this is not the defining energy-per-charge definition of the volt.
options.B: Potential difference is energy per unit charge, so $1 \text{ V} = 1 \text{ J C}^{-1}$ using joule and coulomb.
options.C: Coulomb is charge and ohm is resistance, and there is no direct $V = Q \times R$ definition linking only these two units.
options.D: Coulomb and second define the ampere from $I = Q/t$, not the volt.
